questions.question_text: You are reviewing cases in an addiction clinic. The note in the file says that your next patient  has previously experienced 'formication'. What kind of hallucination is formication?
questions.explanation: A haptic hallucination is a hallucination of touch[cite: 1]. Formication is a form of tactile (or haptic) hallucination in which there is the sensation of numerous insects crawling over the surface of the body[cite: 1]. This is not uncommon in acute organic states, including alcohol or drug withdrawal, particularly from cocaine[cite: 1]. It is a form of superficial hallucination[cite: 1]. The other forms of hallucinations listed above are also superficial hallucinations[cite: 1]. Visceral hallucination is false perceptions of internal organs such as throbbing[cite: 1]. Kinaesthetic hallucination is false perceptions of joint muscles (e.g. twisting or vibrating)[cite: 1]. Hygric hallucination is false perception of fluid[cite: 1]. Thermal hallucination is false perception of hot and cold[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Donna and Malcom have had concerns about their son, Stuart, who is 6 years old and  doesn't seem to be developing social skills in the same way as many of his peers. He dislikes  being in groups, tends to spend a lot of time alone, immersed in quite a narrow repertoire of  interests. If his usual routine is disrupted he can become very upset and difficult to comfort.  Donna and Malcom have been searching the internet, reading about Autistic Spectrum  Disorder, and how it is categorised in diagnostic manuals. Which one of the following  statements is true regarding diagnostic categorisation in ICD and DSM?

options.text: ICD-11 has a category for pervasive developmental disorders
DSM 5 has a category for pervasive developmental disorders
DSM 5 categorises autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) under neurodevelopmental disorders
DSM 5 has a category for overactive disorder associated with mental retardation
DSM 5 includes language development as a core feature of autistic spectrum disorder (ASD)

correct_answer.text: DSM 5 categorises autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) under neurodevelopmental disorders

correct_answers.text: DSM 5 categorises autistic spectrum disorder (ASD) under neurodevelopmental disorders

questions.explanation: DSM 5 describes three 'severity levels' associated with the diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorder[cite: 1]. Diagnostic criteria include persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts; and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities, with symptoms present in the early developmental period and causing impairment in functioning[cite: 1]. For persistent difficulties in the social use of verbal and nonverbal communication, a DSM-5 diagnosis of social communication disorder should be considered[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: John Tulley is known to have epilepsy. On Saturday he attended a live rock concert with  some of his friends. He had one pint of beer to drink. At one point during the concert, he fell  to the ground and began to shake. The appearance was in keeping with a generalised  epileptic seizure. Once the shaking had stopped, John began to regain consciousness. He  sat up and was moving his arms, seemingly without purpose. His speech was not coherent,  and he pursed his lips repeatedly. This lasted for approximately 10 minutes. John didn't recall  this having happened when he was asked about it. What is the term used for this phase?
questions.explanation: The term 'twilight state' describes conditions in which there is a restriction of the morbidly changed consciousness, a break in the continuity of consciousness, and relatively well- ordered behaviour[cite: 1]. If one keeps strictly to these criteria, then the commonest twilight state is the result of epilepsy[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Hana Haq is a 42-year-old woman, who has presented to her GP with features of depression  following the loss of her mother from cancer. For the past month she has been waking up a  few hours earlier than usual. Her appetite has decreased (she has lost half a stone in weight)  and she feels generally demotivated and hopeless, taking little pleasure from her usual  activities. The GP fills out the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAM-D) in order to  ascertain the severity of her depression. Which of the following statements is true of the  HAM-D?

options.text: It does not allow for estimation of severity
It is scored out of a total of 8 points
It excludes behavioural aspects of depression
It has a section on weight loss

correct_answer.text: It has a section on weight loss

correct_answers.text: It has a section on weight loss

questions.explanation: The Hamilton Depression Rating Scale is a widely used scale for measuring depression, consisting of a list of 17 items, designed to be rated by a clinician on three-point and five- point scales[cite: 1]. The symptoms are: depressed mood, guilt feelings, suicide, insomnia (initial or early), insomnia (middle), insomnia (terminal or late), disturbed work and activities, psychomotor retardation, psychomotor agitation, anxiety (psychological), anxiety (somatic), gastrointestinal symptoms, somatic symptoms, sexual dysfunction or menstrual disturbance, hypochondriasis, weight loss, and lack of insight[cite: 1]. The maximum score is 52, and the following interpretation of scores is often used: 10-13 mild depression; 14-17 moderate depression; 18- 30 marked depression; >30 severe depression[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about the diagnosis of delusional disorder?

options.text: ICD-11 requires the symptoms to be present for 6 months
Delusional disorder is associated with mood symptoms
General speech and behaviour are not typically affected
ICD-11 classifies delusional disorder under neurotic disorders
Delusions typically vary from day to day

correct_answer.text: General speech and behaviour are not typically affected

correct_answers.text: General speech and behaviour are not typically affected

questions.explanation: Delusional disorder is characterised by the development of a delusion or set of related delusions, typically persisting for at least 3 months and often much longer, in the absence of a depressive, manic, or mixed mood episode[cite: 1]. The delusions are variable in content across individuals, but typically stable within individuals, although they may evolve over time[cite: 1]. Other characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia (i.e. clear and persistent hallucinations, negative symptoms, disorganised thinking, or experiences of influence, passivity, or control) are not present, although various forms of perceptual disturbances (e.g. hallucinations, illusions, misidentification of persons) thematically related to the delusion are still consistent with the diagnosis[cite: 1]. Apart from actions and attitudes directly related to the delusion or delusional system, affect, speech, and behaviour are typically unaffected[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Bobby is a 22-year-old man, who has been brought to A&E with his mother, following their  involvement in a serious road traffic accident. His mother was very badly injured, and sadly,  whilst in the A&E, she dies. You are asked to go and speak to him. You find him to be in  intense emotional distress: crying, sometimes sobbing, and unable to find coherent words to  express himself. He says that it all feels unreal, and it's as if he's floating outside his body.  What term is most appropriate to describe what is happening to Bobby?
questions.explanation: Acute stress reaction refers to the development of transient emotional, somatic, cognitive, oг behavioural symptoms as a result of exposure to an event or situation (either short- or long- lasting) of an extremely threatening or horrific nature[cite: 1]. Symptoms may include autonomic signs of anxiety (e.g. tachycardia, sweating, flushing), being in a daze, confusion, sadness, anxiety, anger, despair, overactivity, inactivity, social withdrawal, or stupor[cite: 1]. The response to the stressor is considered to be normal given the severity of the stressor (it is not considered a disorder in ICD-11), and usually begins to subside within a few days after the event or following removal from the threatening situation[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Priscilla is a 19-year-old woman whose mother has insisted she come to see you because  she is worried about how thin she is. Priscilla tells you that she doesn't believe herself to be too thin. In fact, she thinks that she could do with losing more weight. She exercises four  times a day, restricts her intake to a couple of apples and half a piece of toast a day. She has  stopped menstruating. Her BMI is 15, and her T3 levels are normal. What's the most likely  diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa is characterised by significantly low body weight for the individual's height, age, and developmental stage that is not due to another health condition or the unavailability of food[cite: 1]. A commonly used threshold is body mass index (BMI) less than 18.5 in adults[cite: 1]. Low body weight is accompanied by a persistent pattern of behaviours to prevent restoration of normal weight, which may include behaviours aimed at reducing energy intake (restricted eating) purging behaviours (e.g. self-induced vomiting, misuse of laxatives), and behaviours aimed at increasing energy expenditure (e.g. excessive exercise), typically associated with a fear of weight gain[cite: 1]. Low body weight or shape is central to the person's self-evaluation or is inaccurately perceived to be normal or even excessive[cite: 1]. T3 levels are not part of the diagnostic criteria; commonly, T3 levels in anorexia nervosa are low, but not in every case[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mr. Phipps is 69 years old, with a history of depression, hypertension and  hypercholesterolaemia. Last week he suffered a stroke affecting his non-dominant  occipitoparietal lobe. You draw Mr. Phipps' attention to objects on a table (a watch, a spoon,  and a plant) and ask him to name them. He tells you he can see a spoon, but nothing else.  When you redirect his attention to the plant, he says that now he does see the plant, but that  he no longer sees the spoon. What term best describes this presentation?
questions.explanation: Simultanagnosia (also called simultagnosia) is a rare neurological disorder characterized by the inability of an individual to perceive more than one single object at a time, and is associated with occipito-parietal lesions[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Miss Hunt is known to the local mental health team, having been diagnosed with a mental  illness by your predecessor. The GP informs you that an ECG has been performed and  shows a prolonged QT interval. You do not have the past notes available to you at this time,  however you know that the following mental health condition is most associated with  prolonged QT interval:
questions.explanation: The starvation effects of anorexia nervosa have consequences on cardiac function and associated with prolonged QT interval[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mr. Nolan is a 35-year-old man who has suffered right cerebral hemisphere damage  following a motorcycle accident. Which of the following symptoms is he most likely to  experience?
questions.explanation: Right hemisphere damage is associated with numerous deficits, including a flat affect and limited emotional expression[cite: 1]. They can also experience deficits in attention, perception, learning, memory, recognition and understanding of para-verbal communication[cite: 1]. They can demonstrate left-sided neglect and hemiparesis[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mrs Oona is a 42-year-old woman who attends her GP describing a sense of feeling her right  arm being pulled and distorted when waking from sleep. Which of the following is the name  for this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: This represents a kinaesthetic hallucination as it involves a sensory disturbance concerning the limbs[cite: 1]. A visceral hallucination would relate to feelings perceived as arising in the viscera and internal organs[cite: 1]. Paraschemazia is characterised by a distortion of a patient's body image[cite: 1]. It can be caused by hallucinogenic drugs such as LSD and mescalin, epileptic auras, and sometimes migraines[cite: 1]. A delusion of control is an abnormality of thought in which a patient believes that their thoughts can be controlled by an external force[cite: 1]. An illusion is a sensory distortion which clear once an individual attend to it, in the case of affect-related or completion illusions, or ignores it, in the case of pareidolia[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Your outpatient mental health service is considering making use of a psychiatric tool in order  to assess presence and severity of mental distress and illness. Someone suggests using the  Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) as a global assessment of symptoms. Which of the  following is true of the BPRS?

options.text: All items are based on the individual's self-report
It includes a section on eating disorders
Items are rated 1-10 in terms of severity
It includes a section on somatic concern

correct_answer.text: It includes a section on somatic concern

correct_answers.text: It includes a section on somatic concern

questions.explanation: The BPRS covers 24 sections/areas of concern, rated in severity 1 to 7[cite: 1]. The first 14 items are based on the individual's self-report, with the remainder on observed behaviour and speech[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: What describes the EEG findings of a patient with delirium?
questions.explanation: Diffuse slowing on an EEG is associated with delirium[cite: 1]. The other findings are described below: Generalised spike wave discharge is seen in tonic clonic epilepsy[cite: 1]. 3 Hz spike wave complex is seen in absent seizures[cite: 1]. Poly spike discharge is seen in myoclonic epilepsy[cite: 1]. Localised rhythmic 5-7 Hz is seen in temporal lobe epilepsy[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Shalinee, a 30-year-old florist, has a history of epilepsy for which she takes carbamazepine.  She is planning to start a family with her husband, David and seeks your advice on  medication during pregnancy. Which of the following pharmacokinetic changes occurs during  pregnancy?

options.text: Reduced absorption from intramuscular site of injection

questions.explanation: Gastric emptying and small intestine motility are reduced in pregnancy due to elevation of progesterone, which tends to reduce absorption via the oral route[cite: 1]. Total body water increases by up to 8 litres, creating a larger space within which hydrophilic drugs may distribute[cite: 1]. Total plasma concentration of albumin-bound drugs decreases as a result of haemodilution and the subsequent fall in plasma albumin concentration and reduced plasma protein binding[cite: 1]. Some enzymes of the hepatic cytochrome P-450 system are induced by oestrogen/ progesterone, resulting in a higher rate of metabolism (and hence elimination) of drugs[cite: 1]. Renal blood flow is increased by 60-80% during pregnancy, and glomerular filtration rate rises by 50%, leading to enhanced elimination of drugs (Dawes 2001)[cite: 1]

questions.question_text: There are numerous specific sub-types of hallucination. Which of the following would  represent an extracampine hallucination?

options.text: A person complaining being able to hear people saying bad things about him from another city
A person feeling that other people can read his mind
A person hearing someone calling his name while falling asleep
A person feeling cold while watching a documentary

correct_answer.text: A person complaining being able to hear people saying bad things about him from another city

correct_answers.text: A person complaining being able to hear people saying bad things about him from another city

questions.explanation: Extracampine hallucinations involve an individual perceiving a voice or auditory stimulus originating from a place which would be out of earshot and thus impossible to actually hear[cite: 1]. The other examples describe reflex hallucinations, hypnagogic hallucinations, thought broadcast and running commentary respectively[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: May is a 78-year-old woman whose husband passed away three weeks ago, following a long  illness. You visit her at home and she talks to you about her experience of loss. Which  feature, following a loss, is usually the most salient?
questions.explanation: According to updated research published in the Journal of the American Medical Association, conducted by the Yale School of Medicine (JAMA 297:Feb 2001), the most salient emotion following loss is yearning[cite: 1]. In the study, Maciejewski said yearning is the defining feature of grief and is an emotion that most clearly reflects the absence of the deceased[cite: 1]. "Yearning is a longing for reunion with the deceased loved one, heartache about an inability to reconnect with this person[cite: 1]. Individuals may cognitively accept the death of a loved one, but they may still pine for them and experience pangs of grief (i.e. yearning)."[cite: 1]

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a true statement of Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS)?

options.text: A symptom of CBS is visual hallucinations of simple repeated patterns
CBS is a form of dementia
CBS can last from a few days to years
A symptom of CBS is complex visual hallucinations
CBS can be caused by cataracts

correct_answer.text: CBS is a form of dementia

correct_answers.text: CBS is a form of dementia

questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet Syndrome (CBS) is not a mental illness, nor a form of dementia[cite: 1]. It is caused by reducing vision in older age such as cataracts or macular degeneration[cite: 1]. The person experiences visual hallucinations out of the blue that can either be simple vivid patterns or more complex visual hallucinations[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a component of schizotypal personality disorder?
questions.explanation: Auditory hallucinations are not associated with schizotypal personality disorder, and more associated with an acute psychotic episode[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: An EEG is performed on a patient of yours who was in REM sleep. Which of the following is  NOT a feature of REM sleep in an EEG?

options.text: Similar activity to an awake state

questions.explanation: REM sleep accounts for 25% of total sleep time in adults and is characterized by high levels of brain activity and physiological activity similar to those seen in wakefulness[cite: 1]. The EEG will show low-voltage and mixed frequency (theta and slow alpha) activity[cite: 1]. Saw-tooth waves are also seen[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mr. Lyons is a man who has been admitted to hospital with a new onset psychotic illness. He  is started on an antipsychotic but then develops confusion, muscular stiffness, marked  sweating and fever. Which of the following factors increases the risk of him developing this  condition?
questions.explanation: A variety of other risk factors have emerged from epidemiological and case studies of NMS which include dehydration, physical exhaustion, exposure to heat, hyponatremia, iron deficiency, malnutrition, trauma, thyrotoxicosis, alcohol, psychoactive substances, and presence of a structural or functional brain disorder such as encephalitis or dementia[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mr. Parson is a man who is referred to a psychiatric clinic with concerns around his cognitive  function. He is sent for an MRI, which demonstrates the 'pulvinar sign' in his thalamus. Which  of the following conditions is he most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation: Variant CJD is associated, in 75% of cases, with the pulvinar sign[cite: 1]. This is bilateral high signal intensities on axial fluid attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) MRI[cite: 1]. Posterior thalami involvement on sagittal T2 sequences is also common[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mrs. Richards is a 32-year-old woman who has been referred to a neurologist for  investigation of possible narcolepsy. Which of the following investigations would be most likely to be used?
questions.explanation: The tests that are commonly used in diagnosing narcolepsy are the polysomnogram, the multiple sleep latency test (MSLT), and administration of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Matilde is an 87-year-old female who is awaiting discharge from the inpatient unit. You  review her medically and notice that her answers, although well formed, are unrelated to your  questions. Her medical history includes hypertension and diabetes. Two years ago she  suffered from a TIA. Comprehension of speech is associated with which part of the cerebral  cortex?
questions.explanation: Wernicke's area is involved in the comprehension of written and spoken language[cite: 1]. It is located in the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the cerebral cortex[cite: 1]. Damage to this area, for example, through infarction, results in a receptive dysphasia whereby patients experience difficulty in understanding language[cite: 1]. The production of speech is not impaired and so the patient is able to speak normally, although the content of their speech is unrelated to the topic of conversation[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: In your CAMHS outpatient clinic, you review Bobby, an 8-year-old boy recently diagnosed  with ADHD. You meet with his parents to discuss your plans to commence methylphenidate  (Ritalin). They are concerned about possible side effects and wish to know more about  these. Which of the following is the most common side effect of methylphenidate?
questions.explanation: Methylphenidate is recommended for use as part of a comprehensive treatment programme for children with a diagnosis of severe attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)[cite: 1]. Common side effects include reduced appetite and insomnia[cite: 1]. Less common side effects include tics or twitches, drowsiness or dizziness, headache, abdominal pain, nausea[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Anna attends a rave where she takes an unknown substance. She later describes the feeling  of her limbs being distorted. Which of the following describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Paraschemazia or body image distortion is the phenomenon of experiencing limbs or other body parts are being distorted; it is commonly seen whilst under the influence of hallucinogens[cite: 1]. Hyposchemazia and aschemazia describe the phenomenon of experiencing limbs that are diminished or absent respectively[cite: 1]. Asomatognosia is the loss of awareness or recognition of a part of the body[cite: 1]. Anosognosia is unawareness of neurological impairment[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Howard is a young man admitted to the ward. He has a diagnosis of schizophrenia and whilst  assessing him, he sweeps your notes off the table onto the floor. On questioning why he did  that, he states that he didn't do it but that something made him. Which of the following  explains the mechanism behind this experience?
questions.explanation: The patient in the vignette above is describing delusions of control[cite: 1]. The phenomenon is explained by altered somatosensory feedback where there is a mismatch between the predicted motor and sensory feedback and the actual feedback[cite: 1]. (Ref: M Wolpert, D & Ghahramani, Zoubin & Jordan, Michael[cite: 1]. (1995)[cite: 1]. An Internal Model for Sensorimotor Integration[cite: 1]. Science (New York, N.Y.)[cite: 1]. 269[cite: 1]. 1880-2[cite: 1]. 10.1126/science.7569931)[cite: 1]

questions.question_text: There are various factors, which influence group dynamics and impact upon their  effectiveness. Which of the following factors can reduce the cohesiveness of a group?
questions.explanation: Role ambiguity refers to the lack of clear definition of what is expected of an individual, with respect to the goals of their team[cite: 1]. The more uncertainty there is about the tasks, goals and levels of performance, the less satisfied workers tend to be[cite: 1]. But in the presence of task and social cohesion job satisfaction improves greatly[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Attention results in the conversion of:

options.text: Short term memory into long term memory
Working memory into short term memory
Sensory memory into short term memory

correct_answer.text: Sensory memory into short term memory

correct_answers.text: Sensory memory into short term memory

questions.explanation: Sensory receptors in the brain are responsible for receiving sensory information which they store for mere seconds[cite: 1]. The brain filters this multifaceted sensory information from multiple sensory organs[cite: 1]. When conscious attention is paid, this certain sensory information is selected and converted into short-term memory which enables us to remember it[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Working memory can be tested at bedside using which of the following?
questions.explanation: Digit span tests working memory by asking the participant to recall sequences of numbers of increasing lengths in a forward or backward manner[cite: 1]. It requires patients to repeat longer strings of digits increasingly as a way of assessing the ability to process relatively simple information[cite: 1]. Cognitive estimation is used to test problem solving[cite: 1]. Wisconsin card sorting test is used to test set shifting[cite: 1]. Stroop test is used to test selective attention[cite: 1]. Clock drawing test is used to test general cognitive ability in dementia[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Which of the following strategies are employed in order to reduce groupthink?

options.text: Focusing on individual successes within the group
Not revealing the roles of individuals within the group
Allowing decisions to be made without criticism

questions.explanation: Groupthink is a collective pattern of defensive avoidance, characteristic of group decision making in organisations in which group members develop rationalisations supporting shared illusions of their own infallibility and invulnerability with the organisation[cite: 1]. Characteristic features include: (1) An illusion of invulnerability; (2) Collective efforts to rationalise in order to discount warnings; (3) An unquestioned belief in the group's inherent morality; (4) Stereotyped views of rivals and enemies; (5) Direct pressure on any member who dissents from the consensus view; (6) Self-censorship of disagreements with the apparent group consensus; (7) A shared illusion of unanimity; and (8) The emergence of self-appointed protectors of the group from adverse information that might undermine the existing complacency[cite: 1]. Appointing a 'devil's advocate' is one strategy that can be employed to reduce groupthink[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Anthony Andrews is a 7-year-old boy who has been displaying some challenging behaviours  at school. His teacher produces a star chart with a star sticker being awarded to Anthony for  good behaviour. Which of the following forms of conditioning would this best fit with?
questions.explanation: Behaviour modification is based on operant conditioning[cite: 1]. Forms of behavioural modification include the use of secondary reinforcement, such as 'token economy', in which socially desirable/acceptable behaviours are rewarded with tokens that can be exchanged for other material items or privileges, or 'star charts' where children's good behaviour is rewarded when a certain level is achieved[cite: 1]. In classical conditioning, stimuli that signal significant events produce reflexive behaviour[cite: 1]. Observational learning is learning that occurs through observing the behaviour of others[cite: 1]. Social conditioning is the sociological process of training individuals in a society to respond in a manner generally approved by the society in general and peer groups within society[cite: 1]. Imprinting describes the phase-sensitive period of a young animal attaching to an external stimulus, usually its mother[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: You are the junior doctor at a unit for severe personality disordered patients, otherwise  known as a therapeutic community. You observe group therapy and attempt to identify group  dynamics based on what you have read in theory. Which of the following best describes  'group cohesion'?

options.text: Quality of the relationship with therapist
Expression of ideas accompanied by emotional response
Group works together towards a common goal

correct_answer.text: Group works together towards a common goal

correct_answers.text: Group works together towards a common goal

questions.explanation: Therapeutic factors in group psychotherapy: Abreaction - Repressed material, particularly a painful experience, is brought back to consciousness[cite: 1]. Acceptance - Feeling of being accepted by other members of the group[cite: 1]. Altruism - Act of one member helping another; putting another's needs before one's own[cite: 1]. Catharsis - Expression of ideas/thoughts/suppressed material that is emotional and produces relief[cite: 1]. Cohesion - Sense that the group is working together toward a common goal[cite: 1]. Consensual validation - Confirmation of reality by comparing own conceptualisations with other group members[cite: 1]. Contagion - Expression of emotion by a member stimulates awareness of similar emotion in another[cite: 1]. Corrective familial experience - Group recreates the family of origin to work through original conflicts psychologically[cite: 1]. Empathy - Capacity of group members to put themselves in psychological frame of another member[cite: 1]. Identification - Unconscious defense mechanism; characteristics of another person are incorporated[cite: 1]. Imitation - Conscious emulation/modeling of one's behaviour after another, 'role modeling'[cite: 1]. Insight - Conscious awareness/understanding of own psychodynamics and maladaptive behaviour[cite: 1]. Inspiration - Process of imparting a sense of optimism to group members; 'instillation of hope'[cite: 1]. Interaction - Free and open exchange of ideas and feelings among group members[cite: 1]. Interpretation - Group leader formulates the meaning of a patient's resistance, defense, and symbols[cite: 1]. Learning - Acquiring knowledge about new areas, such as social skills; receiving advice and obtaining guidance[cite: 1]. Reality Testing - Ability of the person to evaluate objectively the world outside the self[cite: 1]. Transference - Projection of feelings, thoughts, and wishes onto the therapist[cite: 1]. Universalisation - Awareness of patients that they are not alone in having problems; 'self-disclosure'[cite: 1]. Ventilation - Expression of suppressed feelings, ideas, or events to other group members[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Cognitive Estimates Test is used to test the function of which of the following regions of the  brain?
questions.explanation: The Cognitive Estimation Test (CET) is among a number of tests examining executive function[cite: 1]. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) all make up the prefrontal region of the frontal lobe and are all associated with executive functioning but the DLPFC is associated with, among others, problem-solving and abstract reasoning required in the CET[cite: 1]. The ACC is associated with decision-making, motivation and response inhibition and the OFC is associated with impulse control and socially appropriate behaviours[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Amy attends outpatient clinic complaining of discharge from her nipples. Which of the following medications is least associated with this side effect?
questions.explanation: A side effect of antipsychotics can be hyperprolactinaemia[cite: 1]. However, clozapine and aripiprazole are rarely associated with this side effect, and aripiprazole has been shown at low doses to reduce prolactin levels[cite: 1]. This effect is attributed to the D2 receptor partial agonism, which may mitigate the effect of other antipsychotic medications on the pituitary gland[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: You and your colleagues are discussing various aspects of the nature of psychiatry, its  history and current predicaments. One of your colleagues begins to reference a well-known  book by Thomas Szasz. In his seminal book, 'The Myth of Mental Illness', Thomas Szasz  makes which of the following claims?

options.text: Symptoms are explanations for mental illness
There is no such thing as mental illness
All problems in living can be explained by psychochemical processes
The body and mind are separate
Mental illness is a sign of brain disease

correct_answer.text: There is no such thing as mental illness

correct_answers.text: There is no such thing as mental illness

questions.explanation: There were three major themes in Szasz's writings: 1) His contention that there is no such thing as mental illness; 2) His contention that individual responsibility is never compromised in those suffering from what is generally considered as mental illness; 3) His perennial interest in calling attention to the political nature of psychiatric diagnosis[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a component of Kohlberg's conventional stage of morality?
questions.explanation: Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget's concepts and described multiple stages of moral development within three significant levels of morality[cite: 1]. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors[cite: 1]. The second level is morality of conventional role-conformity, in which children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of 'law and order' (authority orientation)[cite: 1]. The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: According to Erikson's stages of psychosocial development, at which stage would a four year old be?
questions.explanation: Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle[cite: 1]. Stage 3 takes place from about 3 years to about 5 years[cite: 1]. Its focus is initiative versus guilt[cite: 1]. The child's increasing mastery of locomotor and language skills expands its participation in the outside world and stimulates omnipotent fantasies of broader exploration and conquest[cite: 1]. Guilt over the drive for conquest and anxiety over the anticipated punishment are both assuaged in the child through repression of the forbidden wishes and development of a superego to regulate its initiative[cite: 1]. Success in this stage will result in development of the basic virtue of purpose[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Mrs. Kean and her 16-year-old son Henry have been having some disagreements about his  future plans. Mrs. Kean has decided which universities Henry will apply for. He protests,  saying he wants to make his own decision, but Mrs. Kean replies saying that the choice is  not his, the decision will be made for him by her and her husband and there's nothing he can  do about it. Henry reluctantly concedes. What parenting style is Mrs. Kean exhibiting?
questions.explanation: Rutter has clustered parenting into four general styles[cite: 1]. The authoritarian style, characterised by strict, inflexible rules, can lead to low self-esteem, unhappiness, and social withdrawal[cite: 1]. Authoritarian parents tend to be restrictive and cold, and their children tend to be withdrawn or conflicted[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Melissa and her partner Jakob have recently had a baby. Jakob is looking forward to charting  their son's development, and wants to draw up a time-line so that he can anticipate what new  skills his son may be able to master. He is anxious to notice any clues that may suggest his  son is not developing as expected. Which of the following scenarios suggests impaired  development?

options.text: Plays with a ball at 16 months

questions.explanation: By age 18 months, a child is generally using 20 single words[cite: 1]. They will understand up to 150 words[cite: 1]. By 24 months, their vocabulary will increase to up to 270 words[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: What type of attachment is demonstrated by a child who seems unaffected by the mother  leaving and carries on playing and also unaffected by the mother's return?
questions.explanation: Mary Ainsworth devised the Strange Situation procedure with 12-to 18-month infants, which categorised infant-parent relationships[cite: 1]. The procedure involves separations and reunions with caregivers and observes response[cite: 1]. In anxious-avoidant attachment, the child seems unconcerned at separation or reunion[cite: 1]. It is associated with unresponsive parenting[cite: 1]. Mary Ainsworth noted that this type of attachment often occurred when the child's needs were repeatedly not met and allows the child to maintain some proximity to the parent without experiencing maternal rejection[cite: 1]. Note that the anxious-avoidant, anxious-resistant and disorganised categories are also described as insecure-avoidant, insecure-resistant (or ambivalent) and insecure-disorganised[cite: 1]. Ainsworth preferred classifications using alphabetical notations (A, B, C)[cite: 1]. The disorganised category is attributed to Ainsworth's student, Mary Main[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Nina and her mother are spending the afternoon together. Nina's mother has been talking  about families. At one point in the conversation Nina asks her mother 'what would happen if I  have a baby brother?' What developmental stage, according to Piaget, is Nina most likely to  be at?
questions.explanation: According to Piaget, the stage of formal operations lasts from about 11 years of age through the end of adolescence[cite: 1]. The stage is so named because young persons' thinking operates in a formal, highly logical, systematic, and symbolic manner[cite: 1]. It is characterised by the ability to think abstractly, to reason deductively, and to define concepts, and also by the emergence of skills for dealing with permutations and combinations[cite: 1]. Adolescents attempt to deal with all possible relations and hypotheses to explain data and events during this stage[cite: 1]. They are able to think abstractly or hypothetically, which is demonstrated by Nina's question[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Kevin is a young boy who is getting into arguments with other children at school and is  occasionally pushing them over. His parents and teachers have attempted to reason with him  but this has not been successful. His behaviour eventually improves when he is told that his  favourite toy will be removed as long as he continues to push others. Which of the following  stages of Kohlberg's moral development would best fit this scenario?
questions.explanation: Lawrence Kohlberg integrated Jean Piaget's concepts and described multiple levels of moral development within three significant levels of morality[cite: 1]. The first level is pre-conventional morality, in which punishment and obedience are the determining factors[cite: 1]. The second level is morality of conventional role-conformity, in which children try to conform to gain approval and maintain good relationships with others and are also guided by rigid codes of 'law and order' (authority orientation)[cite: 1]. The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: In the development of vision, which of the following can be seen occurring as early as the  first day after birth?
questions.explanation: The pupillary light reflex (PLR) whereby the diameter of the pupil is controlled according to the intensity of light occurs from birth[cite: 1]. Depth perception, colour vision and accommodation occur at three to five months[cite: 1]. Convergence occurs at five to seven months[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Anna is 8 years old. You are conducting some exercises to determine what stage of  development she appears to be at, according to Piaget's stages of development. You  present her with two glasses, both of the same shape, and both holding the same amount of  orange juice. You then obtain two other glasses of different shapes: one is tall and thin,  another short and broad. You pour the orange juice from one of the original glasses into the  tall glass, and the juice from the other original glass into the shorter glass. You now ask Anna  to tell you which glass holds the most juice. What answer indicates she has reached the  concrete operational stage of development?

options.text: 'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'
'The short glass has the most orange juice'
'They each have more orange juice than before'
'Glasses can be half empty or half full'
'The tall glass has the most orange juice'

correct_answer.text: 'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'

correct_answers.text: 'Both glasses have the same amount of orange juice'

questions.explanation: According to Piaget, the stage of concrete operations lasts from about 7 to 11 years of age[cite: 1]. In this period, children operate and act on the concrete, real, and perceivable world of objects and events[cite: 1]. Egocentric thought is replaced by operational thought, which involves dealing with a wide array of information outside the child[cite: 1]. Children can now see things from someone else's perspective[cite: 1]. Children also understand the concept of conservation, which is the ability to recognise that, although the shape of objects may change, the objects still maintain or conserve other characteristics that enable them to be recognised as the same[cite: 1]. The ability of children to understand quantity is one of Piaget's most important cognitive developmental theories[cite: 1]. Measures of quantity include measures of substance, length, number, liquids, and area[cite: 1].

The third and highest level is the morality of self-accepted moral principles (post-conventional), in which children voluntarily comply with rules based on a concept of universal ethical principles and make exceptions to rules in certain circumstances[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: The Oedipus complex is associated with which stage of psychosexual development?
questions.explanation: The phallic stage begins sometime during year 3 and continues until approximately the end of year 5[cite: 1]. Threats of castration and the related anxiety are connected with guilt over masturbation and oedipal wishes[cite: 1]. During this phase oedipal involvement and conflict are established and consolidated[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Traditionally, the view has been that boys like to play with cars and girls like to play with  dolls. Which of the following is this an example of?
questions.explanation: Socialisation is the process, beginning in infancy, whereby one acquires the attitudes, values, beliefs, habits, behaviour patterns, and accumulated knowledge of one's society, through child-rearing, education, and modification of one's behaviour to conform with the demands of the society or group to which one belongs[cite: 1]. Indoctrination is the process of inculcating a person with ideas, attitudes, cognitive strategies or professional methodologies[cite: 1]. A stereotype is any thought widely adopted about specific types of individuals or certain ways of behaving intended to represent the entire group of those individuals or behaviors as a whole[cite: 1]. Normalisation refers to social processes through which ideas and actions come to be seen as "normal" and become taken-for-granted or "natural" in everyday life[cite: 1]. Internalisation is an individual's acceptance of a set of norms and values via socialisation[cite: 1].

questions.question_text: Which of Erikson's stages of development are paired correctly?

options.text: 40-65 years old – ego integrity vs. despair

questions.explanation: Erik Erikson created an original and highly influential theory of psychological development and crisis occurring in periods that extended across the entire life cycle[cite: 1]. Stage 3 takes place from about 3 years to about 5 years[cite: 1]. Its focus is initiative versus guilt[cite: 1]. The child's increasing mastery of locomotor and language skills expands its participation in the outside world and stimulates omnipotent fantasies of broader exploration and conquest[cite: 1]. Guilt over the drive for conquest and anxiety over the anticipated punishment are both assuaged in the child through repression of the forbidden wishes and development of a superego to regulate its initiative[cite: 1].
